pros: Guaranteed O(log n) worst-case for all operations
Fewer rotations than AVL during insertion (max 2 vs 1, but simpler fix-ups)
Deletion requires at most 3 rotations (vs O(log n) for AVL)
Battle-tested: used in C++ STL, Java Collections, Linux kernel
Atomic recolorings possible without structural changes
Parent pointers enable efficient iterative traversal
Amortized constant number of structural changes per update
Relaxed balance allows better performance with concurrent access
Can be augmented for order statistics (OS-tree), intervals, etc.
1 bit per node for color (typically packed into existing pointer bits)
Foundation for many real-world systems (schedulers, memory managers)
cons: Taller than AVL trees (2 log n vs 1.44 log n) — slower lookups
Requires parent pointer (extra 8 bytes per node on 64-bit systems)
Debugging is harder due to color invariants
Recoloring cascades can propagate to root (O(log n) recolorings)
Not cache-friendly: pointer chasing causes cache misses
Not suitable for disk-based storage (B-trees are better)
Sequential insertions can create less balanced structure than AVL
Color bit often wastes 7 bits due to byte alignment
More code, more bugs: correct implementation is notoriously difficult
Thread safety requires complex fine-grained locking
Iterative fix-up with parent pointers can be harder to follow than recursion
